title: Opportunistic infections
question: Assign the ICD-10-CM code for the patient's infection (only that code).
note:
Chief Complaint: White patches on the tongue.

Vitals: BP 128/82, HR 74, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 98.6 F.

Recent Labs: eGFR 88 mL/min/1.73m², HbA1c 5.4%, WBC 7.2, Platelets 210k.

Social History: Patient is a 51-year-old male who works as an office manager. He is a non-smoker and drinks alcohol socially. He lives with his spouse and two children.

Family History: Father had hypertension. Mother had hyperlipidemia. No history of significant genetic disorders.

Review of Systems:
Constitutional: Negative for fever, chills, or fatigue.
HEENT: Positive for white plaques on the tongue. Negative for ear pain or vision changes.
Respiratory: Negative for cough or shortness of breath.
Cardiovascular: Negative for chest pain or palpitations.
Gastrointestinal: Negative for abdominal pain or nausea.
Genitourinary: Negative for dysuria.
Musculoskeletal: Negative for joint pain.
Neurological: Negative for dizziness or numbness.

HPI: Patient is a 51-year-old male who presents for a follow-up regarding his chronic respiratory condition. He has been using an inhaled corticosteroid for several months. He reports good control of his baseline symptoms but notes a new development of white patches on his tongue. He denies any difficulty with swallowing.

Exam:
General: Alert and oriented x3, in no acute distress.
HEENT: Oral cavity exam reveals prominent white plaques on the tongue and inner cheeks. These are consistent with oral candidiasis. No signs of active infection or bleeding.
Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm.

Assessment:
1. Oral candidiasis: The patient presents with visible thrush on the tongue, likely secondary to the prolonged use of his inhaled corticosteroid medication. Swallowing remains normal.

Plan:
1. Prescribed Nystatin oral rinse to be used several times daily for 7-10 days.
2. Patient instructed to rinse his mouth with water after each use of his inhaled steroid inhaler to reduce the risk of recurrence.
3. Follow up in 2 weeks to assess resolution of the plaques.

Electronically signed,
J. Lindqvist, NP
October 14, 2026
explanations: Oral thrush: candidal stomatitis, B37.0 (no HCC).
